title: 3H Space Science Mini-Course
summary: Twelve concise lessons that walk through the story of the universe, with embedded quizzes and progress tracking.

lessons.title: Origins: Big Bang to CMB
points: Universe began 13.8 billion years ago in a rapid expansion.
Cosmic inflation stretched space faster than light for a brief instant.
Quantum fluctuations were blown up to cosmic scales.
Matter and antimatter mostly annihilated, a small surplus remained.
Protons and neutrons formed within the first minutes.
Light could not travel freely during the hot plasma era.
At 380k years, electrons and protons combined into atoms (recombination).
Cosmic Microwave Background is the afterglow from that epoch.
Tiny temperature ripples in the CMB seeded all later structure.
Expansion continues today, carrying galaxies apart.

lessons.title: Matter & Energy
points: Ordinary matter is only about 5% of cosmic energy density.
Dark matter (~27%) shapes galaxy rotation and large-scale structure.
Dark energy (~68%) drives the accelerated expansion of space.
Dark matter interacts mainly through gravity, not light.
Galaxy clusters and lensing map dark matter distribution.
Type Ia supernovae revealed accelerating expansion in 1998.
Cosmological constant is a leading dark energy candidate.
Alternatives include dynamical fields that change over time.
The energy budget influences the universe's geometry and fate.
Precision cosmology combines CMB, BAO, and supernova data.

lessons.title: Stars: Birth, Life, Death
points: Stars form when cold molecular clouds collapse under gravity.
Protostars heat up until core fusion ignites (main sequence).
Hydrogen fusion balances gravity with radiation pressure.
Low-mass stars live trillions of years; massive ones burn fast.
Red giants form when hydrogen in the core is depleted.
Fusion shells build heavier elements up to iron in massive stars.
Core-collapse supernovae leave neutron stars or black holes.
Planetary nebulae leave behind white dwarfs for Sun-like stars.
Stellar winds and deaths enrich the interstellar medium.
Star clusters reveal stellar evolution through the HR diagram.

lessons.title: Elements from Stars
points: Big Bang nucleosynthesis made mostly hydrogen and helium.
Stellar cores fuse elements up to carbon and oxygen.
Massive star fusion proceeds to silicon and iron in onion layers.
Iron fusion consumes energy, triggering core collapse.
Supernova shock waves forge elements heavier than iron.
Rapid neutron capture (r-process) creates gold, uranium, and more.
Neutron star mergers also drive r-process enrichment.
Cosmic recycling mixes heavy elements into new star systems.
Your body contains atoms forged in ancient supernovae.
Chemical abundance patterns trace galaxy formation history.

lessons.title: Galaxies: Formation & Structure
points: Dark matter halos are gravitational scaffolds for galaxy growth.
Gas cools and settles into rotating disks inside halos.
Spiral galaxies form stars in disks with arms shaped by density waves.
Ellipticals often result from major mergers that disrupt disks.
Starbursts ignite when gas is funneled inward during interactions.
Supermassive black holes sit at most galaxy centers.
Feedback from stars and black holes regulates star formation.
Galaxy clusters bind hundreds to thousands of galaxies.
Cosmic web filaments channel matter into growing halos.
The Milky Way will merge with Andromeda in ~4–5 billion years.

lessons.title: Black Holes Basics
points: Black holes are regions where escape speed exceeds light speed.
Defined by an event horizon and a central singularity (theory).
Stellar-mass black holes form from collapsing massive stars.
Supermassive black holes reach millions to billions of solar masses.
Accretion disks heat up and emit X-rays and jets.
General relativity predicts time dilation near horizons.
LIGO/Virgo detect black hole mergers via gravitational waves.
M87* shadow imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019.
Hawking radiation implies black holes slowly evaporate.
Information paradox remains an open theoretical puzzle.

lessons.title: Exoplanets & Detection
points: Over 5,000 exoplanets confirmed with multiple methods.
Transit method sees starlight dip as a planet crosses its star.
Radial velocity measures stellar wobble from planet gravity.
Direct imaging captures young or wide-orbit giants in infrared.
Microlensing briefly brightens background stars via gravity.
Astrometry tracks tiny position shifts on the sky.
Habitability depends on temperature, atmosphere, and stability.
Density and spectra reveal composition (rocky, icy, gaseous).
Multi-planet systems show diverse architectures beyond our own.
Future telescopes target biomarkers in exoplanet atmospheres.

lessons.title: Telescopes: Hubble vs JWST
points: Hubble observes mainly visible and ultraviolet light from LEO.
JWST observes infrared light from the Sun–Earth L2 point.
Infrared reveals dust-shrouded regions and early galaxies.
Hubble's 2.4 m mirror vs JWST's segmented 6.5 m mirror.
JWST must stay cold; Hubble relies on servicing missions instead.
Hubble Deep Field pioneered ultra-deep visible imaging.
JWST extends the cosmic frontier to first-light galaxies.
Both telescopes calibrate distance scales and galaxy evolution.
Spectroscopy from both refines exoplanet atmosphere studies.
They are complementary: UV/optical plus IR for full coverage.

lessons.title: Iconic Missions
points: Voyager 1 & 2 are interstellar probes carrying the Golden Record.
Apollo 11 landed humans on the Moon in 1969.
Curiosity rover drills and analyzes rocks on Mars.
Cassini orbited Saturn and probed Titan and Enceladus.
Hubble and JWST are flagship space observatories.
Parker Solar Probe samples the Sun's corona up close.
New Horizons flew past Pluto and into the Kuiper Belt.
International Space Station enables long-term microgravity research.
Sample-return missions are rising (asteroids, soon Mars).
Each mission answers a piece of the cosmic puzzle.

lessons.title: Life & Habitability
points: Habitable zones allow liquid water on rocky worlds.
Magnetic fields and atmospheres shield surfaces from radiation.
Plate tectonics and volcanism recycle nutrients and gases.
Water can also persist in subsurface oceans (Europa, Enceladus).
Biosignatures include gases out of equilibrium (O2 + CH4).
False positives require careful atmospheric context.
Extremophiles on Earth widen the range of possible habitats.
SETI searches for techno-signatures like narrowband radio.
Life may thrive under ice, underground, or in cloud layers.
Future missions aim to sample plumes or return icy moon material.

lessons.title: Future Observatories
points: Next-gen IR/optical telescopes target Earth-like exoplanets.
Large UV/optical/IR (LUVOIR-like) concepts add coronagraphs.
HabEx concepts pair direct imaging with starshades.
Extremely Large Telescopes on Earth push resolution limits.
Gravitational-wave detectors (LISA) will listen in space.
CMB-S4 aims for primordial gravitational wave signatures.
Neutrino and gamma-ray observatories extend multi-messenger reach.
CubeSats and swarm missions add flexibility and cadence.
Interstellar probe concepts explore the heliopause boundary.
International collaboration is key for flagship scale.

lessons.title: FAQ Myths (تصحيح مفاهيم)
points: Myth: "Big Bang was an explosion into space" — it was expansion of space itself.
Myth: "Dark matter is just black holes" — lensing and CMB rule that out for most.
Myth: "Seasons come from Earth–Sun distance" — axial tilt is the driver.
Myth: "Humans only use 10% of the brain" — neuroimaging shows otherwise.
Myth: "The far side of the Moon never sees sunlight" — it does, just not Earth.
Myth: "Space is completely empty" — it has plasma, dust, fields, particles.
Myth: "Black holes suck everything" — only dominate nearby like any gravity well.
Myth: "JWST replaces Hubble" — they are complementary across wavelengths.
Myth: "Life needs sunlight" — chemosynthetic life thrives in darkness.
Myth: "You would freeze instantly in space" — you radiate heat; it takes time.
